title: Danube Drought Shuts Nuclear Plants as Europe Faces Dual Energy Crisis; OPEC+ Caps Output Increases While Supply Routes Stay Disrupted
subhead: Record drought forces Romania to blast rock in the Danube to cool its last nuclear reactor and Hungary faces full shutdown of Paks, while OPEC+ signals its final production hike for 2026 and Trump pressures oil companies over pump prices amid contradictory US-Iran diplomacy signals.

sections.heading: Danube Drought Forces Emergency Nuclear Shutdowns Across Eastern Europe
sections.body:
Romanian military forces detonated 180 kg of explosives to blast a rock outcrop in the Danube River on Monday, attempting to redirect vital cooling water to the country's last operating nuclear reactor at Cernavodă. The extraordinary measure came as record-low water levels forced the shutdown of one of Romania's two reactors, according to The Guardian and Bloomberg.

Across the border, Hungary's Paks nuclear plant — which normally generates nearly half of the country's electricity — is operating at less than 10% capacity and faces full shutdown as early as next week, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced. The 44-year-old Soviet-era facility relies on Danube water for cooling and cannot operate at current river levels.

Serbia's key hydroelectric plant at Đerdap is running at just 20% capacity, prompting an emergency government meeting led by Prime Minister Đuro Macut. All three countries are now relying on expensive power imports as the heatwave simultaneously drives up electricity demand. Hungary's voluntary consumption cuts reduced demand by 700 MW on Sunday, and pharmaceutical company Richter announced it would cut electricity use by more than 50% for three weeks.

No significant rainfall is forecast for the Danube basin in the coming days or weeks, meaning the crisis could deepen further through August.
sections.whyItMatters: The Danube crisis reveals a structural vulnerability in European energy infrastructure: 10 countries depend on the river for power plant cooling, and no contingency exists for sustained drought. With nuclear and hydroelectric output collapsing simultaneously, Eastern Europe faces an energy supply gap that imports alone may struggle to fill — especially with Russian fuel exports banned and LNG markets already tight.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Completes Unwinding of 2023 Cuts, Signals Pause Through Year-End
sections.body:
OPEC+ agreed on Sunday to raise its September production quota by 188,000 barrels per day, completing the phased reversal of the 1.65 million bpd voluntary cut first agreed in 2023. The seven core members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman — approved the increase, but delegates told Reuters and Bloomberg that no further hikes are planned for the rest of 2026, with quotas expected to hold steady from October through January 2027.

In practice, the increase is largely notional. The Strait of Hormuz remains constrained, Russia's output is roughly 9 million bpd against a target of 9.8 million bpd, Kazakhstan has slashed production to about 1 million bpd from over 2 million bpd after drone attacks on Novorossiysk, and Iraq continues to face export constraints. Kuwait's July production surged to 1.971 million bpd from just 580,000 bpd in May, per Reuters — but much of that increase reflects a shift to Red Sea routes rather than a net global supply gain.

A Reuters analysis by Clyde Russell notes the quota hike is 'irrelevant for now' given Hormuz disruptions, but will matter later when shipping normalizes and those barrels actually reach market. The separate, older 2 million bpd OPEC+ production cut remains in place through year-end.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ is out of easy moves. The group has unwound its voluntary cuts on paper, but actual output remains far below quotas due to war-driven disruptions in three member states. The October pause means any further supply relief depends entirely on whether the Strait of Hormuz reopens — handing Tehran continued leverage over global supply.

sections.heading: Trump Demands Oil Companies Cut Gas Prices as Brent Rebounds Above $84
sections.body:
President Trump on Monday publicly demanded that US oil companies immediately lower gasoline prices, singling out Chevron CEO Mike Wirth for criticism. 'Get your consumer (retail!) Oil Prices DOWN, NOW!' Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that without his administration's policies, 'the Oil Industry, and our Country itself, would be DEAD.'

Trump specifically noted that Chevron was thrown out of Venezuela but is now 'back, far bigger and stronger than ever before' under his administration's policy, per Al Jazeera and Oilprice.com. The national average price of regular gasoline stood at about $4.09 per gallon on Monday, per AAA — down only modestly from last week despite crude prices falling more than 6% in a single session.

Oil prices rebounded on Tuesday, with Brent topping $84 and WTI nearing $81, as markets weighed contradictory signals on US-Iran negotiations. The Monday crash followed Trump's announcement that he had called off planned strikes on Iran and said talks would begin. But Iran's Foreign Ministry denied any negotiations with the US, stating it is only discussing Hormuz management with Oman.

This marks Trump's third public intervention on fuel prices. In June, he ordered a Justice Department investigation into gasoline price gouging and urged retailers to push pump prices toward $2.50 per gallon, warning of 'big problems' for non-compliant companies.
sections.whyItMatters: The clash between the White House and oil companies is intensifying ahead of midterm elections. Even with crude falling, retail prices lag due to inventory cycling, and refiners posted banner Q2 earnings on the Iran war premium. Trump's weaponization of Chevron's Venezuela position is a new pressure vector — linking Middle East policy outcomes directly to domestic pump prices.

sections.heading: Iran Denies US Talks Exist as Diplomatic Signals Contradict
sections.body:
A wide gap has emerged between Washington and Tehran's public statements on negotiations. Trump declared on Saturday that 'perimeters of a deal' had been agreed and that negotiations would start Monday, including an 'immediate, complete, and total opening of the Strait of Hormuz' and an end to Iran's nuclear threat, per his Truth Social posts.

But Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that Iranian negotiators are only discussing Hormuz management with Oman, with no talks underway or planned with the US, according to Al Jazeera, Moneycontrol, and Firstpost. Trump subsequently called Iran's leadership 'unbelievably duplicitous' and warned of 'decapitation' if Tehran does not strike a deal.

Gulf stock markets rose on Monday after Trump paused military strikes, with the Dubai bourse outperforming the region, per Reuters. But the lack of confirmed diplomatic progress means the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively disrupted, and shipping insurers are maintaining elevated premiums.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Trump's claims and Iran's stance is not just rhetorical — it means the Hormuz chokepoint remains closed to normal traffic with no timeline for reopening. Until both sides agree on a framework, the 40-50 day mine-clearing timeline reported by Saudi Gazette cannot even begin, and the physical risk premium in oil markets persists.

sections.heading: Ukrainian Drones Drive Russian Refining to 24-Year Low; Russia Extends Fuel Export Ban Through January 2027
sections.body:
Russian oil refining fell to its lowest level in more than two decades in July, processing an estimated 3.6 million bpd — roughly one-third below the seasonal average of 5.3-5.6 million bpd — according to Bloomberg analysis cited by The Moscow Times and Oilprice.com.

Ukraine struck 18 Russian refineries in July, surpassing the previous monthly record of 17 set in May. Targets included the 440,000 bpd Omsk refinery, Russia's largest, over 2,500 km from Ukraine. Ukrainian drones also hit five oil tankers, five pieces of port infrastructure, and two pipelines. Bloomberg counted 30 total attacks on Russian oil infrastructure in July — the second-highest monthly total since the invasion began.

The campaign shifted from refineries in the first half of July to tankers and export logistics later in the month, then back to refineries in the final week, per Carnegie's Sergei Vakulenko. Only four tankers loaded crude at Novorossiysk during the week ending July 26, down from seven to eight in prior weeks.

Meanwhile, Russia has extended its ban on diesel and gasoline exports through January 31, 2027, and is now allowing refineries to produce lower-specification fuel for domestic consumption as shortages mount, per Reuters and Kommersant.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's drone campaign is no longer just knocking out refineries — it is systematically degrading Russia's entire oil logistics chain, from tankers to pipelines to ports. The export ban extension and fuel quality downgrade are signs of genuine domestic supply stress, not just tactical messaging. Russia's ability to offset Black Sea losses through Baltic ports remains limited by pipeline, storage, and tanker constraints.

sections.heading: Dark Tanker Transits Surge at Bab el-Mandeb as Saudi Arabia Reroutes Again
sections.body:
Oil tankers carrying Saudi crude are increasingly transiting the Bab el-Mandeb strait with AIS transponders turned off, according to Oilprice.com and CNBC TV18. Two tankers loaded with 3 million barrels of Saudi oil passed through the Houthi-threatened chokepoint over the weekend with AIS disabled, per TradeWinds.

Saudi Arabia has now been forced to reroute its exports twice: first from Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb, then from Bab el-Mandeb north to the Suez Canal and the SUMED pipeline after Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast. More than half a dozen empty supertankers were en route to Egypt's Sidi Kerir port last week to pick up Saudi crude via the SUMED pipeline, per Bloomberg.

The head of Oilprice.com analysis notes that any oil still flowing via Hormuz is 'considerably lower than pre-war levels,' meaning that even Kuwait's reported production surge to 1.97 million bpd in July reflects Red Sea rerouting rather than net new supply reaching global buyers.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia's double rerouting illustrates how both major Gulf exit routes — Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb — are now compromised. The surge in dark transits, where vessels disable tracking to avoid Houthi targeting, raises both safety and insurance concerns. Each rerouting adds days and dollars to voyages, embedding a structural cost premium into Gulf crude even if military de-escalation materializes.

sections.heading: US-Saudi Nuclear Pact Opens Uranium Enrichment Path Amid Proliferation Concerns
sections.body:
The Trump administration has approved a sweeping nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia that includes a path to domestic uranium enrichment, marking a significant departure from decades of US non-proliferation policy, according to MSNBC and The Daily Press.

The agreement comes as the US wages a war against Iran partly justified by preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, a contradiction that proliferation analysts have highlighted. An editorial in The Daily Press notes the deal 'further erodes safeguards' at a moment when the region's security architecture is already under severe strain.

Separately, Uzbekistan's nuclear power plant project with Rosatom is advancing, with officials stating the first small modular reactor will be commissioned in 2029 and the first large VVER-1000 reactor in 2033. The $9.5 billion project, launched jointly by Putin and Mirziyoyev in June, will produce up to 17 billion kWh annually — roughly 20% of Uzbekistan's electricity needs, per The Diplomat.
sections.whyItMatters: The US-Saudi nuclear deal weakens the non-proliferation argument underpinning the Iran war while creating a new regional enrichment capability. If Saudi Arabia gains enrichment rights, other Gulf states will likely demand equivalent terms, potentially reshaping the Middle East's nuclear landscape for decades. The Uzbekistan-Rosatom project, meanwhile, extends Moscow's nuclear influence across Central Asia.

bottomLine: Eastern Europe's energy crisis intensified as record drought forced emergency measures at two nuclear plants relying on Danube cooling water, while OPEC+ finalized its last scheduled production increase of 2026 — a move that remains largely notional with Hormuz closed, Russia under drone siege, and Kazakhstan's exports hobbled. Trump's contradictory claims of imminent Iran talks were denied by Tehran, leaving the Hormuz reopening timeline uncertain and oil prices volatile. Ukrainian drones drove Russian refining to a 24-year low, Russia extended fuel export bans into 2027, and dark tanker transits surged at Bab el-Mandeb as Saudi Arabia rerouted exports for the second time in months. The common thread: physical supply chains remain deeply disrupted across three theaters, and no diplomatic breakthrough has yet changed that reality on the ground.
sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, Oilprice.com, The Guardian, The Diplomat, Al Jazeera, CNBC TV18, TradeWinds, The Moscow Times, Independent, Daily Press, International Business Times, MSN, Moneycontrol, Firstpost, Yahoo Finance, Rigzone, Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, AAA, Saudi Gazette, Kommersant, The Hans India
